question: Scenario: A healthcare startup wants to build an AI receptionist that handles appointment scheduling, insurance verification, and patient intake over the phone. They have 3 engineers and need to launch in 8 weeks. What architecture do you recommend?
options: LiveKit Cloud with pipeline architecture: Deepgram STT (HIPAA-eligible), Anthropic or OpenAI LLM, Cartesia TTS. A single agent with three tools (schedule_appointment, verify_insurance, collect_intake). SIP trunk via Twilio or Telnyx for phone connectivity. Start simple — one agent, not multi-agent. Add CRM integration in phase 2. LiveKit Cloud removes infrastructure burden for a 3-person team on a tight timeline.

Self-hosted LiveKit with open-source models for HIPAA compliance. Use Whisper (self-hosted) for STT, a locally-deployed Llama model for LLM, and Coqui TTS — all running on the startup's infrastructure. Self-hosting is essential for healthcare because cloud AI providers cannot sign BAAs. This adds 2-3 weeks of setup but ensures regulatory compliance from day one.

GPT-4o Realtime (multimodal) for the lowest latency, paired with a multi-agent architecture: a greeting agent, scheduling agent, insurance agent, and intake agent. The multimodal model eliminates STT and TTS latency entirely. Multi-agent separation ensures each workflow is independently HIPAA-auditable. Use LangGraph to orchestrate the agent state machine.

Start with LiveKit Cloud and the pipeline architecture, but use a dedicated HIPAA-compliant middleware layer between LiveKit and the AI providers. The middleware intercepts all audio and text, strips PHI (Protected Health Information) before it reaches the LLM, and re-inserts it into the response. This allows using any LLM provider without requiring BAAs.
explanation: For a small team with tight timelines: LiveKit Cloud (no infra to manage), pipeline architecture (flexibility to choose HIPAA-eligible providers like Deepgram which does offer BAAs), single agent with tools (simpler than multi-agent), and SIP trunk for phone connectivity. Self-hosting is unnecessary — major cloud providers offer HIPAA-eligible tiers. A PHI-stripping middleware is fragile and unreliable.

question: Scenario: A large insurance company wants to migrate their existing IVR (50 departments, 200 agents) to AI. They handle 10,000 calls/day. How do you phase this migration?
options: Shadow deployment: Route 100% of calls through the AI system but do not let it speak to callers. Instead, the AI silently processes each call, generates what it would have said, and logs it. Human agents handle calls normally. After 4 weeks, compare the AI's suggested responses to what the human agents actually said. Use this data to fine-tune the system before enabling live responses.

Build a complete digital twin of the existing IVR: map every menu tree, every department routing rule, and every agent queue to equivalent AI configurations. Test the digital twin end-to-end with synthetic calls that exercise every path. Once the digital twin passes 99% parity with the existing IVR on the test suite, cut over all 50 departments simultaneously.

Phased migration: (1) Start with 1-2 low-risk departments (e.g., general inquiries) running AI alongside the existing IVR — callers can press 0 to fall back to the old system. (2) Measure task completion rate, escalation rate, and caller satisfaction vs. the old IVR. (3) Expand department by department as each meets quality thresholds. (4) Use the same SIP trunk infrastructure — route a percentage of calls to LiveKit while the rest go to the existing system. Never remove the human escalation path.

Start by replacing only the front-door IVR menu (the first interaction callers have). Keep all department-specific IVR workflows unchanged. The AI handles initial greeting and routing — 'How can I help you today?' — then transfers to the appropriate department's existing IVR tree. This single integration point reduces risk while providing the biggest UX improvement.
explanation: Enterprise migration requires measured, reversible phases. Start with low-risk departments, run AI alongside the existing IVR with a fallback path, and expand based on measured quality. Shadow deployment delays value. A digital twin approach is too rigid. Replacing only the front door leaves 90% of the caller experience unchanged.

question: Scenario: A client's voice agent has 3-second response latency and they want it under 1 second. Where do you look first?
options: Switch to the realtime (multimodal) architecture with GPT-4o Realtime. The pipeline architecture fundamentally cannot achieve sub-1-second latency because three sequential stages (STT + LLM + TTS) each need at least 300-400ms. Multimodal eliminates two stages entirely, making sub-1-second responses achievable. This is the only reliable path to the client's target.

Optimize the network path between the agent and AI providers. Deploy the agent in the same cloud region as your STT, LLM, and TTS providers to minimize inter-service latency. A typical cross-region API call adds 100-200ms; co-locating all services eliminates this overhead at every stage, saving 300-600ms total across the pipeline.

Measure each pipeline stage independently: STT time-to-first-transcript, LLM time-to-first-token, TTS time-to-first-audio. The bottleneck is usually the LLM (slow model or no streaming). Fixes in order of impact: (1) Ensure streaming is enabled on LLM and TTS, (2) Switch to a faster LLM model (e.g., GPT-4o-mini or Claude Haiku instead of full GPT-4o), (3) Consider realtime/multimodal architecture if pipeline latency is fundamentally too high, (4) Optimize agent instructions — shorter instructions mean faster first-token time.

Reduce the agent's system prompt to under 500 tokens. Long system prompts force the LLM to process more context on every turn, increasing time-to-first-token linearly. A 3000-token prompt adds approximately 1-2 seconds of processing time. Refactor detailed instructions into a retrieval tool that provides context only when needed.
explanation: Always measure before optimizing. Break the 3 seconds into STT + LLM + TTS components. The most common culprit is the LLM — either streaming is disabled or the model is too slow. Enabling streaming is usually the single biggest win. Pipeline architecture can achieve sub-1-second latency with streaming enabled and a fast model.

question: Scenario: A client wants both a web-based and phone-based interface for their agent. Should they build two separate agents?
options: No — use the same agent for both. A LiveKit agent sees all callers as room participants regardless of how they connected. A browser user connects via the client SDK. A phone caller connects via SIP trunk -> SIP bridge -> room participant. The agent code is identical. The only difference is the frontend: the web app adds visual UI (transcription, state indicators, text input) that phone callers do not see. One agent, two entry points.

Use the same core agent logic but deploy two variants with different configurations. The phone agent needs G.711 audio handling, DTMF support, shorter response limits (phone callers are less patient), and a simpler persona. The web agent can use higher-quality audio, support text input, and provide richer responses. Shared tools, different agent configurations.

Technically one agent handles both, but best practice is to build channel-aware logic. The agent should detect whether the caller is on phone or web (via participant metadata) and adjust its behavior: shorter responses for phone, visual confirmations for web, DTMF fallbacks for phone users. Without channel awareness, the agent optimizes for neither channel.

Build one agent but use a channel adapter layer. The phone adapter converts G.711 to Opus, handles DTMF events, and manages SIP-specific signaling. The web adapter handles WebRTC negotiation and frontend events. Both adapters present a uniform interface to the agent. This adapter pattern keeps the agent simple while handling channel-specific complexity.
explanation: This is a key LiveKit architectural insight. The SIP bridge converts phone callers into standard room participants. The agent does not know or care whether it is talking to a browser or a phone — it publishes and subscribes to audio tracks either way. One agent codebase serves both channels. Channel-specific adaptation is handled by the SIP bridge, not the agent code.

question: Scenario: A client wants their agent to support English, Spanish, and Mandarin. What are the architectural implications?
options: Use a real-time translation pipeline: always process audio in English (using English-optimized STT and LLM), then translate the LLM's English response into the target language before TTS. This approach uses the best-performing English models and adds a translation step. Translation adds 200-300ms but ensures consistent LLM quality across all languages.

Deploy three separate agent instances, each configured for one language with language-optimized STT, TTS, and agent instructions. Use a lightweight language detection model at the SIP/entry layer to route callers to the correct language-specific agent. This ensures each language gets the best possible provider configuration without runtime switching complexity.

Language support affects every pipeline node. STT must support the target languages (check provider coverage — not all support Mandarin well). The LLM must generate responses in the detected language (most major LLMs handle this). TTS needs voices for each language (check provider voice libraries). Agent instructions should specify multilingual behavior: detect the caller's language and respond in kind. Consider a language detection step early in the call to select the optimal STT model and TTS voice.

Use a multilingual multimodal model (GPT-4o Realtime) that handles all three languages natively in audio-to-audio mode. This eliminates the need to select language-specific STT and TTS providers entirely. The model detects the language from the audio input and responds in the same language. Pipeline architecture cannot handle multilingual requirements effectively.
explanation: Multilingual agents require consideration at every pipeline stage. STT accuracy varies by language and provider. LLMs handle multiple languages well but need explicit instructions. TTS requires language-specific voices. A translation layer degrades quality and adds latency. Separate agents per language add unnecessary operational complexity. Pipeline architecture handles multilingual effectively with proper provider selection.
